findings.title: Unsafe attribute checking via `hasattr` in `has_read`
findings.description: The `has_read` function relies on `hasattr(obj, "read")`. According to Python documentation, `hasattr` triggers `__getattr__` and `__getattribute__` on the object. While `__getattr__` is only called when standard lookup fails, the change in `models.py` replaces `isinstance(data, SupportsRead)` with this function. This allows objects with a `__getattr__` proxy mechanism to pass the check even if they don't truly implement the `SupportsRead` protocol. If an attacker can influence the object being passed as `data`, they could potentially trigger arbitrary code execution within the `__getattr__` implementation during the `hasattr` call, or bypass intended type constraints.
findings.suggestion: Instead of `hasattr(obj, "read")`, perform a safe check that does not execute arbitrary `__getattr__` logic for security-sensitive paths, or verify that `read` is actually a callable method expected on the specific object type. For generic inputs, restrict `has_read` to explicit duck-typing checks that verify `callable(getattr(obj, 'read', None))` and handle `AttributeError` safely without relying on `__getattr__` to define security-relevant behavior. Given this is a library used for HTTP requests, strict adherence to the `SupportsRead` protocol is preferable to loose attribute checks.
